s0201.literal: Our house has for two generations served as Shixing commandery; lingering care remains among the people—we may rightly go south to preserve the family line.
s0201.idiomatic: Our family has held Shixing commandery for two generations, and the people still cherish us. We should go south and keep the line alive.

s0202.literal: " Thereupon together with his younger brother Tong and more than a hundred clansmen and kin he fled to the Lingnan region.
s0202.idiomatic: " He then fled to Lingnan with his brother Tong and more than a hundred kinsmen.

s0203.literal: At the time Ouyang Hao of Shixing was inspector of Hengzhou; Yin went to rely on him.
s0203.idiomatic: Ouyang Hao of Shixing was then inspector of Hengzhou, and Yin went to join him.

s0204.literal: Hao was later transferred to Guangzhou, died of illness, and his son He took command of his following.
s0204.idiomatic: Hao was later moved to Guangzhou, died there, and his son He took over his forces.

s0205.literal: Yin often suspected He of ulterior intent; because of affairs he admonished and corrected him, and from this ritual feeling gradually grew distant.
s0205.idiomatic: Yin often suspected He of hidden designs and tried to correct him when occasions arose, so their courtesy grew strained.

s0206.literal: When He raised troops in rebellion, the capital literati Qin Zhijing, Gongsun Ting, and others were all terrified and alarmed; only Yin was at ease, and said to Zhijing and the others: "Guan Ning and Yuan Xi too merely sat quietly.
s0206.idiomatic: When He rebelled, the capital scholars Qin Zhijing, Gongsun Ting, and others were all in terror; only Yin was calm. He told Zhijing and the rest, "Guan Ning and Yuan Xi too only sat still.

s0207.literal: The gentleman straightens the person to illuminate the Way, makes himself upright to enact righteousness—what need is there for worry and fear?
s0207.idiomatic: A gentleman sets his person right to show the Way and keeps himself straight to act with righteousness—what is there to fear?

s0208.literal: " When Zhang Zhaoda pacified Panyu, Yin at last returned north.
s0208.idiomatic: " After Zhang Zhaoda pacified Panyu, Yin at last came back north.

s0209.literal: Emperor Xuan summoned Yin to question him on affairs beyond the ranges; Yin stated the whole course from beginning to end; the emperor was greatly pleased and that same day invested him as vice minister of the gold office.
s0209.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan summoned Yin to ask about the south. Yin laid out the whole story; the emperor was delighted and that day made him vice minister of the gold office.

s0210.literal: Yin was skilled at clerical script and was valued by his age.
s0210.idiomatic: Yin excelled at clerical script and was highly regarded in his day.

s0211.literal: Emperor Xuan once spread out memorials for business; pointing to Yin's signature he said: "This character's brush momentum is fluttering, like a bird about to fly.
s0211.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan once went through memorials and, pointing to Yin's signature, said, "The brushwork is light and swift, like a bird about to take flight.

s0212.literal: " Yin thanked him, saying: "This is Your Majesty lending it feathers.
s0212.idiomatic: " Yin replied, "That is because Your Majesty lent it feathers.

s0213.literal: " He also said to Yin: "Whenever I am angry, on seeing you my mind is eased—why?
s0213.idiomatic: " He also asked Yin, "Whenever I am angry, seeing you calms me. Why is that?

s0214.literal: " Yin said: "This is because Your Majesty does not shift anger; how could your servant share in this grace?
s0214.idiomatic: " Yin said, "Your Majesty does not vent anger on others. How could a subject claim credit for that?

s0215.literal: " In the seventh year of Taijian he was given the added rank of martial-awe general.
s0215.idiomatic: " In Taijian year 7 he was given the added rank of martial-awe general.

s0216.literal: In the ninth year he was made staff adviser to the Prince of Shixing, central guard, and concurrently vice minister of the gold office.
s0216.idiomatic: In year 9 he was made staff adviser to the prince of Shixing in the central guard and kept the gold-office vice ministry.

s0217.literal: Yin's nature was upright and unyielding; he did not serve the powerful; to close attendants at court he made no visits of request; whenever Emperor Xuan wished to promote him, he was at once cut short by those in power.
s0217.idiomatic: Yin was upright and would not court the powerful; he never paid calls on the emperor's intimates. Whenever Emperor Xuan meant to advance him, the men in power blocked it.

s0218.literal: When the army was destroyed at Lülü Mountain and military stores stood empty, he was transferred to vice minister of the storehouse office, in charge of manufacturing bows, crossbows, spears, arrows, and the like.
s0218.idiomatic: After the disaster at Lülü Mountain left the arsenals bare, he was moved to vice minister of the storehouse office to oversee the making of bows, crossbows, spears, and arrows.

s0219.literal: Yin held office one year, and weapons and gear were fully stocked.
s0219.idiomatic: Within a year the armory was full again.

s0220.literal: He was repeatedly given the posts of secretariat vice minister, steadfast-prestige general, and yellow-gate gentleman.
s0220.idiomatic: He was repeatedly promoted to secretariat vice minister, steadfast-prestige general, and yellow-gate gentleman.

s0221.literal: In the twelfth year the vice ministry of personnel was vacant; the relevant offices repeatedly recommended Wang Kuan, Xie Xie, and others; the emperor used none of them and by personal edict appointed Yin.
s0221.idiomatic: In year 12 the personnel vice ministry fell vacant. The offices kept recommending Wang Kuan and Xie Xie, but the emperor would not use them and by personal edict named Yin.

s0222.literal: At the time Ma Jing, inspector of Guangzhou, had won the hearts of the people beyond the ranges; his arms were drilled and keen; every year he penetrated deep into Liao caves; he also had repeated battle merit; court and countryside alike grew uneasy.
s0222.idiomatic: Ma Jing, inspector of Guangzhou, then held great sway in the south. His troops were well trained, he raided deep into Liao territory every year, and he won battle after battle, so court and countryside alike grew uneasy.

s0223.literal: Emperor Xuan, because Yin knew conditions beyond the ranges thoroughly, also sent Yin to observe Jing, examine his conduct, and hint that he should send hostages.
s0223.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan knew Yin understood the south and sent him to watch Ma Jing, judge his conduct, and urge him to send hostages to court.

s0224.literal: Yin received the secret charge and went south, outwardly using collection and supervision of tribute goods as his pretext.
s0224.idiomatic: Yin took the secret order south, publicly claiming to collect and oversee tribute goods.

s0225.literal: When he reached Panyu, Jing at once grasped the intent and sent all his younger brothers down to the capital as hostages.
s0225.idiomatic: At Panyu Jing saw through the mission at once and sent all his younger brothers to the capital as hostages.

s0226.literal: On returning to the Gan River, Emperor Xuan died; Houzhu succeeded; Yin was transferred to junior mentor of the heir apparent and left office on grounds of illness.
s0226.idiomatic: On his way back at the Gan River, Emperor Xuan died and Houzhu took the throne. Yin was made junior mentor of the heir apparent but resigned on grounds of illness.

s0227.literal: The next year there were many thieves in the capital region; he was again raised as steadfast-prestige general and magistrate of Jiankang.
s0227.idiomatic: The next year, with theft rife in the capital, he was recalled as steadfast-prestige general and magistrate of Jiankang.

s0228.literal: At the time, within the palace halls
s0228.idiomatic: At the time, within the palace halls

s0230.literal: [team] captain Wu Jin, [14] and the eunuchs Li Shandu, Cai Tuo'er, and others repeatedly pressed requests for favors; Yin refused every one.
s0230.idiomatic: [team] captain Wu Jin [14] and the eunuchs Li Shandu and Cai Tuo'er pressed many private requests; Yin refused them all.

s0231.literal: Yin's clansman Mi was then a yellow-gate gentleman; he remonstrated with Yin, saying: "Li and Cai's power—those in office all fear them; you too ought to make some allowance for yourself.
s0231.idiomatic: Yin's kinsman Mi, then a yellow-gate gentleman, urged him: "Everyone in office fears Li and Cai. You ought to look out for yourself a little.

s0232.literal: " Yin said: "In establishing myself I have my own root and branch; how could I change my conduct for Li and Cai?
s0232.idiomatic: " Yin said, "I have my own principles. How could I change my ways for Li and Cai?

s0233.literal: Even if it goes badly, at most I lose my post.
s0233.idiomatic: If things go badly, I lose my post—that is all.

s0234.literal: " Wu Jin in the end composed an anonymous letter; Li and Cai bore witness; on this charge he was dismissed from office and died at home, aged fifty-eight.
s0234.idiomatic: Wu Jin then sent an anonymous accusation, which Li and Cai backed. Yin was removed from office, died at home, and was fifty-eight.

s0235.literal: His son Deyan was the most renowned.
s0235.idiomatic: His son Deyan was the best known.

s0236.literal: Among Yin's clansmen and younger kinsmen, many were known for righteous conduct.
s0236.idiomatic: Many of Yin's clansmen were known for upright conduct.

s0237.literal: His younger brother Tong, through quiet ease and love of learning, reached the posts of junior mentor of the heir apparent and chief steward to the Prince of Nankang.
s0237.idiomatic: His brother Tong, quiet and studious, rose to junior mentor of the heir apparent and chief steward to the prince of Nankang.

s0238.literal: Mi, styled Shiji, was clever and keen from childhood, broadly learned, and had literary talent.
s0238.idiomatic: Mi, styled Shiji, was clever as a boy, widely read, and gifted in letters.

s0239.literal: His grandfather Chen was Liang special advance.
s0239.idiomatic: His grandfather Chen had been Liang special advance.

s0240.literal: His father You was director of the palace workshops.
s0240.idiomatic: His father You was director of the palace workshops.

s0241.literal: In the eighth year of Taijian Mi was made acting attendant-in-ordinary and sent on embassy to Qi.
s0241.idiomatic: In Taijian year 8 Mi served as acting attendant-in-ordinary on embassy to Qi.

s0242.literal: He successively held the posts of yellow-gate vice minister, junior mentor of the heir apparent, and attendant-in-ordinary.
s0242.idiomatic: He later held the posts of yellow-gate vice minister, junior mentor of the heir apparent, and attendant-in-ordinary.

s0243.literal: The historiographer says: Xie, Wang, Zhang, and Xiao all took purity and quiet as their wind; elegance and refinement flowed in reputation; though they met many hardships, in the end they achieved a name.
s0243.idiomatic: The historiographer says: Xie, Wang, Zhang, and Xiao all made purity their manner and won fame for culture. Though hardship followed them, they still made their names.

s0244.literal: Huan's blunt remonstrance in office and heroic wind that shook the vulgar—examining his conduct, he was indeed an ancient's lingering care left behind [15].
s0244.idiomatic: Kong Huan's blunt honesty in office and heroic bearing that stirred the age show, on review, the lingering goodwill of the ancients [15].

s0245.literal: Gu's plain vegetables and Chan delight [16]—such men were beyond the vulgar; yet they still met entanglement in dismissal and fear of ruin.
s0245.idiomatic: Wang Gu lived on plain food and Chan devotion [16], men above the common run, yet even they were snared in dismissal and feared collapse.

s0246.literal: From this one knows the power of Shangguan and Bolu, the shock of Yan, Deng, Liang, and Dou—how dreadful!
s0246.idiomatic: So one sees how fearsome were the powers of Shangguan and Bolu and the tremors of Yan, Deng, Liang, and Dou.

s0248.literal: The Founder as [south] inspector of Xuzhou—Zhang Senkai's collation note says: "According to the Founder's annals, it should read 'inspector of South Xuzhou.'
s0248.idiomatic: On "the Founder as [south] inspector of Xuzhou": Zhang Senkai's collation note says the Founder's annals require "inspector of South Xuzhou."

s0249.literal: " It is now supplied on that authority.
s0249.idiomatic: South is now supplied on that authority.

s0250.literal: In old times Lu Jia on the southern campaign and Zhao Ta's submission—"Zhao Ta" in all editions reads "Zhao Tuo."
s0250.idiomatic: On "Lu Jia's southern campaign and Zhao Ta's submission": all editions read Zhao Tuo.

s0251.literal: Present examination: the graphs tuo and ta share sound and are used interchangeably; Zhao Tuo's "tuo" in the Lunheng chapters "On Nature" and "On Rebuke" both write "ta."
s0251.idiomatic: Tuo and ta are homophones used interchangeably; Zhao Tuo's tuo appears as ta in the Lunheng chapters On Nature and On Rebuke.

s0254.literal: [zhou]—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0254.idiomatic: [zhou]—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0255.literal: According to the Houzhu annals, in the third year of Zhide, Xie Zhou of the left-household ministry was made minister of personnel—"zhou" is also written wrongly as "shen," already corrected on the authority of the Southern Supervisory edition.
s0255.idiomatic: The Houzhu annals for Zhide year 3 name Xie Zhou of the left-household ministry as minister of personnel; zhou is also miswritten shen and is already corrected in the Southern Supervisory edition.

s0256.literal: Here the Southern Supervisory edition is also wrong; therefore it is changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0256.idiomatic: Here the Southern Supervisory edition is also wrong, so the History of the Southern Dynasties is followed.

s0257.literal: Minister of Education Wang Sengbian with a report
s0257.idiomatic: On "Minister of Education Wang Sengbian with a report"

s0259.literal: [memorial] submitted and heard—changed according to Comprehensive Mirror 413 and 754.

s0260.literal: According to the History of the Southern Dynasties it reads "with a report submitted," without the character "heard."
s0260.idiomatic: The History of the Southern Dynasties reads "with a report submitted," without heard.

s0261.literal: Also repeatedly granted the rank of marquis of Wuxi and Jiaxing counties—the Imperial Overview 642 citation and Comprehensive Mirror 209 and 303 all lack the character "marquis"; the History of the Southern Dynasties also lacks "marquis"; the character "marquis" is suspected as a spurious addition.
s0261.idiomatic: On "also repeatedly granted the rank of marquis of Wuxi and Jiaxing counties": Imperial Overview 642 and Comprehensive Mirror 209 and 303 omit marquis, as does the History of the Southern Dynasties; marquis is probably a spurious addition.

s0264.literal: Chong's [grandson]—according to Zhang Chong's biography in the Book of Southern Qi, Zhicai was his grandson.
s0264.idiomatic: On "Chong's [grandson]": Zhang Chong has a biography in the Book of Southern Qi; Zhicai was his grandson.

s0265.literal: The character "grandson" should stand below the character "of"; all editions are alike in error; it is now moved to the correct place.
s0265.idiomatic: Grandson should follow the particle zhi; all editions err; the word is now placed correctly.

s0266.literal: Grand master of the great fleet—the Southern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions read "grand master of the great storehouse," suspected as a later man's reckless change.
s0266.idiomatic: On "grand master of the great fleet": the Southern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions read grand master of the great storehouse, probably a later corruption.

s0267.literal: See collation note five in the biography of Cai Jingli in scroll sixteen.
s0267.idiomatic: See collation note 5 in the biography of Cai Jingli, scroll 16.

s0268.literal: About to be executed on the charge—the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "the whole faction was executed."
s0268.idiomatic: On "about to be executed on the charge": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "the whole faction was executed."

s0271.literal: [uncle] Zuo—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0271.idiomatic: [uncle] Zuo—emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0272.literal: Right vice director of the masters of writing—according to the biography of Xiao Sihua in the Book of Song it says "summoned as left vice director of the masters of writing, firmly declined and did not accept investiture"—thus Sihua never was right vice director of the masters of writing.
s0272.idiomatic: On "right vice director of the masters of writing": the Book of Song biography of Xiao Sihua says he was summoned as left vice director and firmly declined, so he never held the right post.

s0273.literal: Enfeoffed as Duke Mu of Yang—the biography of Xiao Sihua in the Book of Song shows Sihua inherited the rank and was enfeoffed as marquis of Yang county; on death his posthumous title was Mu.
s0273.idiomatic: On "enfeoffed as Duke Mu of Yang": the Book of Song biography of Xiao Sihua shows he inherited and was enfeoffed marquis of Yang county; his posthumous title was Mu.

s0275.literal: In the third year of Tianjia summoned as junior mentor of the heir apparent—below it again says "in the third year, made steadfast-prestige general and assistant magistrate of Danyang," so one of the two "third year" readings must be wrong.
s0275.idiomatic: On "in Tianjia year 3 summoned as junior mentor of the heir apparent": below it again says "year 3, made steadfast-prestige general and assistant magistrate of Danyang," so one of the two year-3 notices must be wrong.

s0278.literal: [uncle] Xiu—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0278.idiomatic: [uncle] Xiu—emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0279.literal: At the time, within the palace halls
s0279.idiomatic: At the time, within the palace halls

s0281.literal: [team] captain Wu Jin—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0281.idiomatic: On "[team] captain Wu Jin": emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0282.literal: He was indeed an ancient's lingering care left behind—Zhang Senkai's collation note says "lingering care" should read "upright legacy left behind."
s0282.idiomatic: On "he was indeed an ancient's lingering care left behind": Zhang Senkai's collation note says lingering care should read upright legacy left behind.

s0283.literal: Present examination: Zhang's view is correct.

s0284.literal: Kong Huan's biography: Emperor Wen said, "The upright legacy of the ancients is seen again in you"—therefore the historiographer cited it.
s0284.idiomatic: Kong Huan's biography records Emperor Wen saying, "The ancients' upright legacy appears again in you," which the historiographer echoed here.

s0285.literal: Gu's plain vegetables and Chan delight—"Chan delight" in all editions reads "cicada slough."
s0285.idiomatic: On "Gu's plain vegetables and Chan delight": all editions read cicada slough.

s0286.literal: According to examination, Chan delight is Buddhist terminology.

s0287.literal: The biography says he revered the Buddhist Law; when he completed mourning for his birth mother he thereafter for life ate only vegetables; at night he sat in Chan; by day he chanted Buddhist sutras.
s0287.idiomatic: The biography says he devoutly followed Buddhism; after mourning for his birth mother he ate only vegetables for life, sat in meditation at night, and chanted sutras by day.

s0288.literal: Therefore to write "Chan delight" is correct.
